routes.description: Establish that consciousness, intentionality, agency, and personal identity cannot be exhausted by physical descriptions, then identify a single nonphysical subject capable of persisting independently of its present body and entering later embodiment.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the mental features and identity conditions require a nonphysical bearer, bodily dependence is compatible with that bearer's continued existence, and a coherent mechanism or argument supports survival beyond bodily death.

motionBridge.description: Show that a conscious person includes one nonphysical subject whose identity can continue after the present organism dies.

centralBridges.description: Establish that phenomenal character or intrinsic intentionality is not captured by an exclusively physical inventory.
Connect irreducible mental properties to a single subject that bears and unifies the person's mental states.
Supply identity conditions under which that subject can remain the same person across bodily discontinuity or renewed embodiment.
Explain why dependence of embodied capacities on the brain does not entail destruction of the subject when the brain ceases functioning.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use reason-responsive agency or freedom to reinforce the distinction between mentality and bottom-up physical causation.
Provide cosmological or probabilistic support for recurrence or another opportunity for postmortem embodiment.

routes.description: Account for consciousness, intentionality, agency, and personal unity as properties or activities of natural organisms at appropriate explanatory scales, while challenging any inference from mental distinctiveness to a separable enduring substance.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic organism-level explanations accommodate the cited mental phenomena, brain dependence undermines an independently functioning bearer, and the proposed identity or cosmological grounds for postmortem survival are not required.

motionBridge.description: Show that the conscious person is a natural organism and that no independently surviving nonphysical subject is needed.

centralBridges.description: Explain mental properties at the organismic scale without reducing them to microphysical vocabulary or adding another substance.
Give physicalist-compatible accounts of phenomenal knowledge, intentional attitudes, and unified consciousness.
Use the systematic dependence of mental capacities on brain states and integrity to oppose separable personal existence.
Challenge the identity conditions and cosmological premises offered to support recurrence or postmortem persistence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve deliberation and reason-responsive action through compatibilist or higher-scale causal explanation.
Relate the onset and loss of conscious capacities to the presence of suitable neural organization.

sections.title: Phenomenal consciousness and physical explanation
sections.rationale: The status of qualia and phenomenal knowledge determines whether first-person experience supplies evidence for facts or properties beyond a natural physical account.

sections.title: Intentionality, mental causation, and agency
sections.rationale: Competing accounts of aboutness, reason-responsive action, and higher-level causation test whether mental activity requires a nonphysical source or fits an organismic framework.

sections.title: From nonphysical properties to subjects and personal identity
sections.rationale: The motion concerns substances rather than merely unusual properties, making the inference to a unified subject and its criteria of persistence an indispensable burden.

sections.title: Cosmology, recurrence, and postmortem survival
sections.rationale: The temporal probability argument, recurrence mechanism, and rival cosmological models bear on whether personal existence can recur after bodily death.

sections.title: Brain dependence, embodiment, and disembodied capacity
sections.rationale: Evidence concerning brain impairment, suitable neural conditions, and the capacities of a disembodied subject bears directly on separability and survival.
